summary: The MEF Forum defined a rooted-multipoint Ethernet service called E-Tree, where leaves talk to roots but not each other. This document describes how to provide the service using Ethernet VPN and PBB-EVPN, building on the framework in RFC 7387.

plainLanguage.summary: In a company, many workers can talk to the boss, but the workers cannot talk to each other. This does that on a network.

questions: what is a leaf label in evpn
how does evpn filter leaf to leaf traffic
what is the e-tree extended community
subtitle: How EVPN lets leaf sites reach root sites but never each other, by tagging MAC addresses and BUM traffic.

tldr.problem: The MEF E-Tree service lets Root sites talk to everyone but forbids Leaf sites from talking to each other, and a provider needs to build that on an EVPN or PBB-EVPN network.
tldr.mechanism: PEs mark MAC addresses learned from Leaf sites with a new E-Tree extended community so the ingress PE can drop Leaf-to-Leaf unicast, and BUM traffic from Leaf sites carries a Leaf label so egress PEs can filter it.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 7385 by using the top bit of the PMSI Tunnel Type field, and it filters known unicast earlier than the VPLS approach in RFC 7796.

today: RFC 8317 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 7385 by using the most significant bit of the PMSI Tunnel Type field.

sections.title: The E-Tree Service and Why EVPN
sections.content:
The MEF Forum defined a rooted-multipoint Ethernet service called Ethernet-Tree (E-Tree). Each customer site, usually an Attachment Circuit (AC) such as an 802.1Q VLAN tag, is labeled either Root or Leaf. Root sites can talk to every other site. Leaf sites can talk to Root sites but not to other Leaf sites.

RFC 7387 gives the framework for E-Tree over MPLS. This document meets those requirements using EVPN (RFC 7432) and PBB-EVPN (RFC 7623), with some extensions. Because EVPN learns MAC addresses in the control plane through BGP, filtering of known unicast traffic can happen at the ingress PE instead of at the egress PE as in the VPLS solution of RFC 7796. Knowledge of RFC 7432 is a prerequisite.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a classroom where every student may talk to the teacher but not to each other. Doing the checking at the start, before a note is passed along, saves a lot of walking around.

sections.title: Three Root and Leaf Scenarios
sections.content:
The RFC groups E-Tree deployments by how Root and Leaf roles are assigned:

  • Per PE: a given EVPN Instance (EVI) on a PE has only Root ACs or only Leaf ACs. Two Route Targets (RTs) per EVI can be used, one for Root and one for Leaf. A PE with Root sites imports both, while a PE with only Leaf sites imports only the Root RT. Split-horizon filtering blocks Leaf AC to Leaf AC traffic on the same PE.
  • Per AC: one EVI on a PE can have both Root and Leaf ACs, so remote MAC addresses must be colored as Root or Leaf before being advertised.
  • Per MAC address: an AC carries both kinds of sites and the role is tied to each MAC address. This is not covered by RFC 7387 or MEF 6.1. Only known unicast is supported, and BUM traffic is dropped by the ingress PE.

For coloring, approach A always uses two RTs and approach B uses a single RT plus a color flag in a new extended community. Approach B is chosen and recommended across all three scenarios, because it keeps RT usage consistent with baseline EVPN. If many PEs end up with both Leaf and Root sites, a single RT per EVI should be used.
sections.plainLanguage: You can decide who is a boss or a worker by whole buildings, by each door, or by each person. The RFC picks one way of putting name tags on people that works for all three.

sections.title: Known Unicast: Filtering at the Ingress PE
sections.content:
A PE MUST tell other PEs whether its MAC addresses belong to Root or Leaf sites. It does so by advertising a Leaf-Indication flag, carried in the new E-Tree extended community, with each MAC/IP Advertisement route learned from a Leaf site. No flag means the MAC address belongs to a Root site.

On the ingress PE, the destination MAC lookup returns the forwarding adjacency plus that flag. The PE compares the flag with the status of the originating AC, and if both are Leaf the packet is not forwarded. This avoids sending the packet across the MPLS/IP core just to be discarded at the far end.

If a MAC address moves between Leaf and Root sites, the MAC mobility procedures in Section 15 of RFC 7432 take precedence to find where the MAC is before it is associated with a Root or Leaf role.
sections.plainLanguage: Each address on the list gets a sticker saying Leaf or not. Before sending, a worker checks both stickers, and if both say Leaf, the note never leaves the building.

sections.title: BUM Traffic and the Leaf Label
sections.content:
Broadcast, unknown unicast and multicast (BUM) traffic goes to many destinations, so it cannot be filtered at the ingress PE. This specification relies on egress filtering instead. MPLS frames that come from a Leaf AC MUST carry a Leaf label, which works in the data plane like the ESI label of RFC 7432. The Leaf label is allocated per PE, independent of ESI and EVI. It can be upstream assigned for P2MP LSPs or downstream assigned for Ingress Replication tunnels.

Single-homed Leaf sites use one Leaf label per PE, advertised in the E-Tree extended community on an Ethernet Auto-Discovery per ES (EAD-ES) route with an ESI of zero. A PE that receives this label blocks the packet if the destination AC is a Leaf and forwards it otherwise. Traffic from Root ACs, single-homed or multihomed, follows the plain RFC 7432 procedures with no Leaf label. For multihomed Leaf sites, the Leaf label alone is enough, including for the Leaf AC on the same Ethernet Segment.

The ingress PE also puts all its Leaf ACs of a bridge domain into a single split-horizon group, which blocks forwarding among them for both BUM and known unicast traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: A shout to the whole room cannot be checked in advance, so the shout carries a Leaf badge. Each listener who is also a Leaf simply ignores any shout wearing that badge.

sections.title: How PBB-EVPN Does It
sections.content:
In PBB-EVPN the Root or Leaf indication rides on the Backbone MAC (B-MAC) address. The same E-Tree extended community is advertised with the MAC advertisement route. When a multihomed Ethernet Segment has both Root and Leaf sites, two B-MAC addresses are used: one per ES, which implicitly means Root, and one per PE, which is tagged with the Leaf-Indication flag. The ingress PE picks the source B-MAC based on the Ethernet Tag of the frame. A PE also advertises two global B-MAC addresses, one Root and one Leaf, for single-homed segments.

Known unicast is filtered at the ingress PE: the C-MAC lookup yields the target B-MAC plus a Root or Leaf flag, and Leaf-to-Leaf traffic is not forwarded. BUM traffic is filtered at the egress PE using a list of source B-MAC addresses, built with the same logic as the split-horizon filtering in Section 6.2.1.3 of RFC 7623, so no extra data-plane flag is needed. Without MAC learning, filtering is done at egress PEs only.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of a badge on each message, the sender uses one of two return addresses, a Leaf one or a Root one. Receivers just look at the return address to decide whether to throw it away.

sections.title: BGP Encoding
sections.content:
The E-Tree extended community is a new transitive extended community with Type 0x06 (EVPN) and Sub-Type 0x05, encoded in 8 octets. It carries one flags octet, whose lowest bit is the Leaf-Indication (L) flag, and a Leaf label field.

  • With a MAC/IP Advertisement route: L is set to one, the Leaf label SHOULD be zero, and the receiver MUST ignore the label. An L value of zero here is invalid and an error should be logged.
  • With an EAD-ES route (ESI of zero): the Leaf label MUST be a valid MPLS label, encoded in the high-order 20 bits of the field, and the receiver MUST ignore the flag.

The RFC also defines a composite tunnel bit, the high-order bit of the Tunnel Type in the PMSI Tunnel attribute. When set, the Tunnel Identifier starts with a three-octet label. A Root PE uses this to signal a P2MP tunnel for sending and an Ingress Replication tunnel for receiving. PEs that do not understand the bit treat the attribute as malformed. The bit is invalid with Tunnel Types 0x00 and 0x06. IANA allocated sub-type 5 and created an E-Tree Flags registry, and the PMSI Tunnel Types registry changed accordingly.
sections.plainLanguage: The Leaf sticker is a tiny 8-byte tag with a few boxes to tick. One box says this one is a Leaf, and another holds a ticket number used when shouting to the room.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 7432 and RFC 7623 apply here too. The Root and Leaf designation is an added check, because it lets the operator stop traffic exchange among Leaf sites through ingress filtering for known unicast and egress filtering for BUM traffic.

An AC with no Leaf designation is treated as Root for backward compatibility. So to avoid traffic between Leaf ACs, the operator SHOULD configure the AC with the right role before activating it.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone without a badge is treated as a boss by default. So hand out the badges before opening the doors.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: One octet; the L bit is the Leaf-Indication.

fields.name: Leaf Label
fields.desc: MPLS label in the high-order 20 bits, used with EAD-ES routes.
